country.name: Chile
country.summary: Chile is a long, thin wine country held between the Andes and the Pacific, with the Atacama desert to the north and cold rain to the south. That isolation kept phylloxera out, so most vines grow on their own roots. The Humboldt Current runs cold up the coast, so a vineyard near the sea is cool whatever its latitude, while the inland valleys are warm, dry and irrigated from Andean snowmelt. Cabernet Sauvignon from the Maipo is the benchmark red, Carménère the signature grape, and Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Casablanca, San Antonio and Limarí the cool face of the country. The law of 1994 maps origin as region, subregion, zone and area; since 2011 a label may add Costa, Entre Cordilleras or Andes to say where between the ranges the fruit grew. Variety, vintage and origin each need 75 per cent, 85 for the European Union.
country.overview:
The vine came with the Spanish in the middle of the sixteenth century, and for three hundred years Chilean wine meant País, the grape Spain calls Listán Prieto, California calls Mission and Argentina calls Criolla Chica. The turn came in 1851, when Silvestre Ochagavía brought French cuttings to his estate near Santiago, about a dozen years before phylloxera was first seen in France. The great houses of the century belong to the same era: Carmen, Cousiño Macul, San Pedro, Errázuriz, Santa Carolina, Santa Rita, Concha y Toro and Undurraga were all founded between 1850 and 1885. Carménère came with those cuttings and survived here after it all but vanished from Bordeaux. The modern era opened in 1979, when the Torres family of Penedès arrived at Curicó with stainless steel, and the 1990s export boom followed. A French ampelographer identified Carménère among the Merlot in 1994, and the variety entered the official register in 1998. The Berlin Tasting of January 2004 set the icon tier on world lists.

The geography is a ribbon some four thousand kilometres long and rarely two hundred wide. Two gradients explain the wine. From north to south, rainfall rises: Coquimbo cannot carry a crop without irrigation, the Central Valley irrigates from Andean snowmelt, and from Maule south the coastal hills can be dry farmed. From east to west matters more. The cold Humboldt Current pushes fog inland at dawn, so a vineyard near the ocean ripens weeks later than one at the same latitude behind the Coastal Range, and the Andean foothills are cooled again by mountain air at night. Between the two ranges lies the Central Depression, warm, flat and fertile. Soils follow position: alluvial gravels on the Andean fans, decomposed granite on the Coastal Range, clay on the floor, and limestone, rare in Chile, best known in Limarí.

The law rests on Ley 18.455 of 1985 and on Decreto 464 of 1994, which drew the map of origin. Six viticultural regions run north to south: Atacama, Coquimbo, Aconcagua, Valle Central, Sur and Austral. Each holds subregions, the valleys, and some hold zones and areas. In 2011 the complementary terms Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes were added, climate words that may follow a valley's name. A decree of 25 May 2018 created four areas, Apalta, Los Lingues, Lo Abarca and Licantén, each needing 85 per cent from the named ground; new varieties were announced in July 2024, and an amendment of May 2025 wrote Chiloé into the Austral region. Variety, vintage and origin each need 75 per cent, 85 for the European market; wine must reach 11.5 per cent alcohol; the Reserva words exist but ask little.

The exam leans on a short list: Maipo and Puente Alto for Cabernet, Colchagua and Apalta for Carménère, Casablanca and Leyda for Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, Limarí for Chardonnay, the Carménère story, phylloxera's absence, the 75 and 85 per cent rules, the three position terms, and the old País and Carignan of the dry south.
ladder: The six broad regions of Decreto 464: Atacama, Coquimbo, Aconcagua, Valle Central, Sur and Austral. Rarely on a label except as Valle Central for a blend across valleys.
The valley, and the working origin a server names: Elqui, Limarí, Aconcagua, Casablanca, San Antonio, Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule, Itata, Bío Bío, Malleco.
A division of a valley: Cachapoal and Colchagua within Rapel, Leyda within San Antonio, Teno and Lontué within Curicó, Claro, Loncomilla and Tutuvén within Maule.
The smallest unit, usually a commune: Puente Alto, Pirque, Peumo, Santa Cruz, Molina, Cauquenes. The 2018 areas Apalta, Los Lingues, Lo Abarca and Licantén must be 85 per cent from the named ground.
Complementary terms since 2011 for position between the ranges: coast, the central depression, the Andean foothills. They describe climate and rank nothing.
A special denomination for País or Cinsault from listed dry-farmed communes of the southern Coastal Range; the term is reserved for those two grapes.
Reserva, Reserva Especial, Reserva Privada, Gran Reserva

Label terms with light conditions: Reserva and Reserva Especial at 12 per cent alcohol, Reserva Privada and Gran Reserva at 12.5, with the Especial and Gran tiers asking some oak. A house's habit says more than the word.
A stated variety, vintage or origin must reach 75 per cent of the blend; wine for the European Union is held to 85.
labels: DO, Denominación de Origen
The origin statement of Decreto 464: a region, valley, zone or area that is true for at least 75 per cent of the wine.
Viña
A winery or wine estate; the usual first word of a house's name.
Valle
Valley; Valle del Maipo, Valle de Colchagua, Valle de Casablanca are the subregions.
Costa
A coastal site, cooled by the Pacific; may follow the valley name.
Entre Cordilleras
Between the ranges, the central depression; the warmest position.
Andes
The Andean foothills; cold nights, stony soils.
Reserva, Gran Reserva
Legal terms with light demands on alcohol and oak; not a quality rank.
Envasado en origen
Literally bottled at origin; a bottling statement, not a quality term.
Secano
Dry farmed, without irrigation; Secano Interior is a protected term for País and Cinsault.
Pipeño
The country wine of the south, young and unfiltered, from País or Cinsault, traditionally sold in bulk.
Cosecha
The vintage; must be 75 per cent true.
Carménère
Chile's signature grape, sold as Merlot until 1994; often written Carmenere on a Chilean label.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The most planted grape and the benchmark red: cassis, cedar and a mint or eucalyptus edge from the Maipo, riper and rounder from Colchagua.

grapes.name: Carménère
grapes.styles: The signature grape, late ripening, with red fruit, paprika, soy and a green pepper note when picked early; best from Peumo, Apalta and Isla de Maipo.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: The cool coastal white of Casablanca, San Antonio, Leyda and Limarí: grapefruit, nettle, salt and sharp acidity.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Restrained and mineral from Limarí and the coast, fuller from the warmer valleys; the Malleco plateau makes a southern version of real tension.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Soft, plummy reds from the Central Valley; its history is tangled with Carménère, which it was mistaken for.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Two faces: peppery and savoury from the coast and from Elqui and Limarí, dense and chocolatey from Colchagua and Cachapoal.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Light to medium reds of red cherry and spice from Casablanca, Leyda, San Antonio, Limarí and Bío Bío.

grapes.name: País
grapes.styles: The colonial grape, light, pale and rustic from old dry-farmed bush vines in Itata and Maule, now made with care as pipeño and as serious light red.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Planted in the south after the 1939 earthquake; pale, juicy, peppery reds from old bush vines in Itata.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Old dry-farmed bush vines of the Maule secano: dark, high acid, savoury reds under the VIGNO banner.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: A supporting red in Colchagua and Maule blends, occasionally bottled alone with a floral, plummy character.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A cool southern speciality of Bío Bío, dry and lime scented, with scattered coastal plantings.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Moscatel de Alejandría: the pisco grape of the north and, from old Itata vines, a dry aromatic white sometimes made on its skins.

exam: Know the six viticultural regions of Decreto 464 and which valleys each holds; the Central Valley's four, Maipo, Rapel, Curicó and Maule, are the likeliest ask.
Tie each benchmark to its address: Puente Alto for Cabernet, Peumo and Apalta for Carménère, Casablanca and Leyda for Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir, Limarí for Chardonnay.
Hold the Carménère story in three dates: the 1850s arrival, 1994 identification, 1998 registration, and why it tastes green when picked with Merlot.
Know the 75 per cent rule and its 85 per cent export version, the 11.5 per cent minimum alcohol and the four Reserva words.
Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes: the year, 2011, and that they describe position, never quality.
Phylloxera's absence, own-rooted vines and the geographic walls that explain it.
At Advanced, the 2018 areas, the Secano Interior rule, the Berlin Tasting result and the old País, Cinsault and Carignan vineyards of the south.
traps: Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes are climate and position terms, never a quality ladder; a Maipo Andes is no better in law than a Maipo Costa.
Reserva and Gran Reserva are defined in Chilean law but ask only for a little alcohol and some oak; do not read them as Rioja's ageing tiers.
Carménère was sold as Merlot until 1994 and ripens weeks later; a green, herbaceous Chilean Merlot of the old days was usually Carménère picked too soon.
Latitude misleads: Casablanca and Leyda lie level with the warm Maipo yet are cool, because the sea and the fog, not the latitude, set the climate.
Rapel is the legal valley; Cachapoal and Colchagua are its zones, and most labels name the zone, so a server rarely sees Rapel on a bottle.
País is not a Chilean native: it is Listán Prieto, Spain's grape, the same as California's Mission.
The 75 per cent rule is Chilean law; a bottle on an American or European list may well have been made to the 85 per cent standard instead.

questions.q: Which grape was sold as Merlot in Chile until it was identified in 1994?
questions.exp: Carménère came from Bordeaux in the 1850s mixed with Merlot cuttings and was grown and labelled as Merlot until a French ampelographer identified it in 1994; it entered the official register in 1998.

questions.q: Which ocean current cools Chile's coastal vineyards with morning fog?
questions.exp: The Humboldt Current carries cold water up the Chilean coast and pushes fog inland at dawn. The Benguela cools South Africa's west coast, the California Current the Pacific coast of North America, and the Agulhas warms South Africa's east.

questions.q: What minimum share of a wine must a stated grape variety reach under Chilean law?
questions.exp: Decreto 464 asks 75 per cent for a stated variety, vintage and origin alike. Wine for the European Union is made to that market's 85 per cent rule, so both figures appear in study material.

questions.q: In which year did Chilean law add Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes as label terms?
questions.exp: The three complementary terms were added in 2011 to say where between the ranges the fruit grew. 1994 is the origin decree itself, 2004 the Berlin Tasting and 2018 the year four new areas were gazetted.

questions.q: Which viticultural region of Decreto 464 holds the Maipo, Rapel, Curicó and Maule valleys?
questions.exp: The Central Valley region runs Maipo, Rapel, Curicó and Maule from north to south. Aconcagua holds Aconcagua, Casablanca and San Antonio; Coquimbo holds Elqui, Limarí and Choapa; Sur holds Itata, Bío Bío and Malleco.

questions.q: Under what name does Chile grow the grape California calls Mission?
questions.exp: País is Listán Prieto, the Spanish grape the missionaries carried through the Americas; it is Mission in California and Criolla Chica in Argentina, and it was Chile's main grape for three centuries.

questions.q: In which year was Decreto 464, the decree that drew Chile's map of denominations of origin, issued?
questions.exp: Decreto 464 of 1994 drew the regions, subregions, zones and areas; some books give 1995, the year it took effect. Ley 18.455 of 1985 is the wider law it rests on, 2011 added the position terms and 2018 created four new areas.

questions.q: Which vine pest has never established itself in Chile's vineyards?
questions.exp: Phylloxera never took hold, so most Chilean vines are own-rooted: desert, mountains, ocean and strict quarantine kept it out. Root-knot nematodes and mealybugs are long established, and the European grapevine moth was found in Chile in 2008.

regions.name: Elqui / Limarí
regions.summary: Elqui and Limarí are the two wine valleys of the Coquimbo region, Chile's north, around 30 to 31 degrees south, with the smaller Choapa a third. Rain is scant, so every vine drinks from a river and a reservoir. Elqui is the pisco valley, a narrow cleft climbing from La Serena into the Andes, where Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc now grow at altitude under the clearest skies in the country. Limarí is broader, centred on Ovalle and open to the sea, where the camanchaca fog and limestone, rare in Chile, give Chardonnay, Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc a taut, saline cut. Hold the pair as cool north, sun with fog, never as hot desert.

terroir.climate: Semi-desert. Rainfall is scant, around 100 millimetres a year or less, falling in winter and heavier in an El Niño year. Sunshine is near constant and the ultraviolet light fierce, yet the valleys are cooler than the latitude suggests: Elqui by altitude and the mountain air that drains down the valley at night, Limarí by the camanchaca, the low cloud the Humboldt Current pushes inland each morning. The swing from day to night is wide inland and holds the acidity.
terroir.soils: Elqui's floor is alluvial sand and stone washed down a steep valley, poor and free draining, with scree on the terraces above. Limarí is the exception in a country of granite and gravel: a layer of calcium carbonate, left by an ancient sea, lies over clay and alluvium around Ovalle and on the coastal Talinay hills, and growers credit it with the valley's mineral edge.
terroir.topography: Elqui is a narrow corridor running east from the coast at La Serena past Vicuña and Paiguano into the Andes, with vineyards from the lower valley to above 2,000 metres at Alcohuaz, among the highest in Chile. Limarí is a wider basin around Ovalle, with a Coastal Range low enough to let the fog through and the valleys of the Hurtado and Grande rivers feeding it from the mountains. Choapa, to the south, sits at the narrowest point of the whole country.
terroir.water: The Elqui river, held at the Puclaro reservoir, and the Limarí river, fed by the Hurtado and the Grande, whose reservoirs include La Paloma, are the whole of the water: there is no vineyard here without a canal or a drip line. The Pacific, a short drive west, supplies fog rather than rain, and the fog is the cooling.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The red that made both valleys' reputations: white pepper, violet and blackberry from the Elqui heights, meatier and more saline from fog-cooled Limarí.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Limarí's signature white, grown on the calcareous soils near the coast: lemon, oyster shell and a chalky grip with modest oak.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Sharp, citrus and herb scented whites from both valleys, with a salty finish where the fog reaches.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: A newer planting on Limarí's coastal limestone: pale, red fruited and savoury.

grapes.name: Carménère
grapes.styles: Grown in Elqui's warmer middle reaches for spicy, ripe reds and for blending with Syrah.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A small share in both valleys, firm and herbal, mostly for blends.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Moscatel de Alejandría and Moscatel Rosada are the backbone of pisco, the grape spirit of the north, with a little dry white from table vineyards.

grapes.name: Pedro Jiménez
grapes.styles: A pisco grape, neutral and productive, grown on pergolas along the Elqui floor; it is not the Pedro Ximénez of Jerez in character or use here.

wines.note: Medium to full, peppery and floral, with fresh acidity from altitude and firm but fine tannin; serve at cellar temperature with lamb, grilled sausage or a peppered steak.
Lean and mineral, lemon and wet stone over a saline finish, oak kept in the background; a match for oysters, ceviche and crab.
Grapefruit, green herb and a salty edge, drier and less pungent than Casablanca; pour cold with shellfish and raw bar dishes.
Light, red cherried and earthy from the coastal limestone, best lightly chilled with salmon, duck or mushroom dishes.

made.viticulture: Nothing grows here without water, so the vineyard begins at the canal. Drip irrigation is universal, water rights are the scarce asset, and a dry year is managed by cutting the crop before cutting the vine. Table grapes and pisco vines fill the Elqui floor on parrón pergolas; the wine vineyards climb the terraces and side valleys, where the vertical trellis is the rule and the rows are set to put leaf between the fruit and a sun that burns at this altitude. Elqui's wind, which rises each afternoon along the corridor, dries the canopy and keeps disease away but demands windbreaks and a careful choice of aspect. In Limarí the fog hangs until late morning, shortening the sun's hours and letting growers plant Chardonnay and Pinot Noir within sight of the sea at Talinay. Soils are thin and alkaline where the carbonate lies, so vigour is low and yields modest without effort. Harvest runs from February for the whites to April for Syrah, earlier than the latitude would suggest a southern reader to expect.
made.winemaking: Syrah is picked for freshness rather than weight, often fermented with a share of whole bunches and raised in large or used oak, so the pepper and violet show over the fruit; the highest Elqui estate treads its grapes by foot in stone lagares and presses by hand. Limarí Chardonnay is often barrel fermented with its lees but with little new wood, malolactic conversion held back to keep the lemon and chalk, and concrete eggs are common for the same reason. Sauvignon Blanc is made cold and reductively in steel, picked for acidity rather than pungency. The north's older trade is pisco: Muscat, Pedro Jiménez and Torontel are fermented dry and distilled in copper stills, and the spirit has carried a denomination of origin since 1931, limited to the Atacama and Coquimbo regions. A server who knows the pisco sour's origin knows why the Elqui valley was planted long before anyone thought of Syrah.

law.classification: The Coquimbo viticultural region of Decreto 464 holds three subregions: Valle del Elqui, Valle del Limarí and Valle del Choapa. Elqui's areas are Vicuña and Paiguano; Limarí's are Ovalle, Monte Patria, Punitaqui and Río Hurtado; Choapa's are Salamanca and Illapel. North again lies the Atacama region with the Copiapó and Huasco valleys, planted mostly for pisco and table grapes. A label may add Costa, Entre Cordilleras or Andes after the valley name under the 2011 rules, where the decree allows it, and in these narrow valleys the coast and the high terraces are truly different places. Pisco's own denomination of origin dates from 1931 and covers only the Atacama and Coquimbo regions, among the oldest such protections in the Americas. Variety, vintage and origin each need 75 per cent.

labels: Camanchaca
The coastal fog of the north; a word growers use to explain why Limarí is cool.
Pisco
Grape brandy of the Atacama and Coquimbo regions, protected since 1931.

places.name: Elqui Valley
places.note: The northernmost of the atlas valleys, a corridor from La Serena to the Andes known for pisco, clear skies and astronomical observatories. Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc and Carménère grow on the terraces; the higher, the cooler and the more peppery the Syrah.

places.name: Vicuña
places.note: The valley's main town and an area of the decree; the first serious wine estate of the valley opened here in 1998 on the floor and lower slopes.

places.name: Paiguano
places.note: The upper area of the decree, also written Paihuano, where the valley narrows and the side valleys climb; the gateway to the highest vineyards.

places.name: Alcohuaz
places.note: A hamlet in the upper Elqui whose terraced vineyards rise above 2,000 metres, among the highest in Chile; Syrah, Garnacha and other Mediterranean grapes trodden by foot in stone lagares.

places.name: Limarí Valley
places.note: A broad basin around Ovalle, south of Elqui, where the fog reaches far inland and calcium carbonate lies in the soil. Chardonnay, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir with a mineral, saline signature; the north's most important fine wine valley.

places.name: Ovalle
places.note: The valley's centre and an area of the decree, on the Limarí river below the La Paloma reservoir; most of the valley's wineries sit around it.

places.name: Talinay
places.note: Low coastal hills within sight of the Pacific, about a dozen kilometres from the sea, where limestone outcrops and the fog sits longest; the source of the valley's most mineral Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Monte Patria
places.note: An inland area up the Grande river, warmer and sunnier, planted to Syrah, Cabernet and table grapes.

places.name: Río Hurtado
places.note: The area along the Hurtado river to the north east, high and dry, with small plantings of Syrah and pisco grapes.

places.name: Punitaqui
places.note: The area south of Ovalle towards the Coastal Range, dry and hilly, with scattered vineyards.

places.name: Choapa Valley
places.note: The third Coquimbo subregion, around Salamanca and Illapel, where the Andes and the sea nearly meet and Chile is at its narrowest; a few stony vineyards, Syrah chief among them, rarely seen abroad.

places.name: Atacama region
places.note: The Copiapó and Huasco valleys north of Coquimbo: pisco and table grapes in true desert, with a handful of table wines from the Huasco coast; an Advanced curiosity rather than a Certified question.

producers.name: Viña Falernia
producers.why: Founded in 1998 at Vicuña, the estate that proved Elqui could make fine Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc rather than pisco alone.

producers.name: Viñedos de Alcohuaz
producers.why: Among the highest vineyards in Chile, above 2,000 metres in the upper Elqui, with Syrah trodden by foot and pressed by hand.

producers.name: Viña Tabalí
producers.why: The Limarí house whose Talinay vineyard on coastal limestone defined the valley's mineral Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Concha y Toro
producers.why: The Maipo giant farms in Limarí and draws its finer Chardonnay from the valley; Maycas del Limarí was its label for the valley's wines.

producers.name: De Martino
producers.why: The Maipo house that has bottled Syrah from Elqui and from Choapa, a useful side by side of the north.

exam: Place Elqui and Limarí in the Coquimbo region, north of Aconcagua, with Choapa as the third valley.
Limarí's limestone and camanchaca fog explain its Chardonnay; Elqui's altitude explains its Syrah.
Pisco: the 1931 denomination, the Atacama and Coquimbo regions, the Muscat family grapes.
The areas of the decree are an Advanced ask: Vicuña and Paiguano; Ovalle, Monte Patria, Punitaqui and Río Hurtado.
Alcohuaz, among Chile's highest vineyards, is a Master-level detail worth one card.
traps: The north is not hot desert wine: fog and altitude make Elqui and Limarí cool valleys, and the whites taste of it.
Limarí's calcium carbonate is a local exception; most of Chile grows on granite, gravel and clay.
Pisco's denomination is Chilean law of 1931 and is separate from Peru's claim to the same name; the exam asks the Chilean regions, Atacama and Coquimbo.
Elqui lies north of Limarí; the atlas sheet runs north to south and the pair is named in that order.
Pedro Jiménez is a pisco grape, not the sherry grape by use, even though the names are near twins.

cards.b: Chile's northernmost fine wine valley and pisco country: the Andes corridor east of La Serena, Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc at altitude under cloudless skies, irrigated from the Elqui river.
A broad valley around Ovalle, open to the camanchaca fog, with calcium carbonate in the soil: taut Chardonnay, peppery Syrah, saline Sauvignon Blanc.

cards.b: Camanchaca: low cloud pushed inland by the cold Humboldt Current; it burns off by late morning and cuts the sun's hours.

questions.q: Which Chilean valley is known for a layer of calcium carbonate beneath its vineyards?
questions.exp: Limarí's soils around Ovalle and at coastal Talinay carry calcium carbonate left by an ancient sea, rare in Chile. Elqui is alluvial sand and stone, Maipo is Andean gravel and Colchagua is clay and granite.

questions.q: Which spirit holds a denomination of origin shared by Chile's Atacama and Coquimbo regions?
questions.exp: Chilean pisco has carried a denomination since 1931 for the Atacama and Coquimbo regions, distilled from Muscat family grapes. Singani is Bolivia's Muscat brandy, cachaça Brazil's cane spirit and grappa Italy's pomace brandy.

questions.q: What is the name of the morning fog that cools Limarí's vineyards?
questions.exp: The camanchaca is the low coastal cloud the Humboldt Current pushes inland each morning; it hangs over Limarí until late morning and shortens the sun's hours, which keeps the whites fresh.

questions.q: Which viticultural region of Chile's 1994 decree holds Elqui, Limarí and Choapa?
questions.exp: Coquimbo is the northern wine region of Decreto 464 with those three valleys. Atacama lies further north with Copiapó and Huasco, Aconcagua holds Casablanca and San Antonio, and the Valle Central runs from Maipo to Maule.

questions.q: Which red grape leads the fine wine of the Elqui valley?
questions.exp: Syrah from Elqui's high terraces, peppery and floral, made the valley's reputation after 1998. Cabernet and Carménère are minor plantings there, and Pinot Noir belongs to Limarí's coastal limestone.

questions.q: Which white grape is the signature of the Limarí Valley?
questions.exp: Chardonnay from Limarí's calcareous soils and fog-cooled slopes near the coast, as at Talinay, is the valley's signature: lemon, chalk and a saline cut. Riesling and Gewürztraminer are southern specialities of Bío Bío, and Viognier is a minor Chilean planting.

questions.q: Which valley is the third subregion of the Coquimbo region, alongside Elqui and Limarí?
questions.exp: Choapa, around Salamanca and Illapel where Chile is at its narrowest, completes Coquimbo's three subregions and is a small source of stony Syrah. Copiapó and Huasco, further north, belong to the Atacama region.

regions.name: Aconcagua / Casablanca
regions.summary: The Aconcagua viticultural region holds three valleys that must be studied apart. The Aconcagua valley proper follows its river from the Andes north of Santiago to the sea: warm and inland at Panquehue, home of Errázuriz, and at Ocoa, where Seña grows, both for Cabernet blends; cool and schisty at Aconcagua Costa. Casablanca, in the Coastal Range west of Santiago, was planted in 1982 for the sea fog and became Chile's first cool white valley: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. San Antonio and its Leyda zone lie closer to the Pacific again and make the country's sharpest Sauvignon Blanc and most savoury Pinot Noir and Syrah. The Humboldt Current is the teacher here, not the latitude.

terroir.climate: Three climates. Inland Aconcagua at Panquehue is warm Mediterranean, dry, sunny and sheltered, ripening Cabernet with ease. Casablanca is cool Mediterranean: fog fills the basin at dawn, the sea breeze arrives after noon, the harvest runs two to three weeks behind the Maipo and spring frost is the chronic hazard. San Antonio and Leyda are cooler and windier still, a dozen kilometres from the water, with cloud that can sit all morning and a growing season that stretches into April for Pinot Noir.
terroir.soils: The Aconcagua floor is alluvial, with colluvial slopes of clay and stone on the hills where the serious Cabernet is planted; near the coast the bedrock is schist and slate, unusual in Chile. Casablanca sits on decomposed granite with pockets of clay and sandy loam, thin and poor on the slopes, deeper on the floor. San Antonio and Leyda are granite under red clay, shallow and free draining, which with the wind keeps vigour low.
terroir.topography: The Aconcagua valley runs east to west, from the high Andes near the border to the sea at Concón, so a label's Costa or Andes tells a true story about position. Casablanca is a basin inside the Coastal Range at 200 to 400 metres, open to the sea through gaps on its western side, its eastern end warmer and nearer Santiago. San Antonio is rolling coastal hill country south of Casablanca; Leyda's vineyards sit on low coastal ridges, and Lo Abarca is a bowl barely four kilometres from the surf.
terroir.water: The Aconcagua river, fed by Andean snowmelt, irrigates the interior and is the reason it was planted in the nineteenth century. Casablanca has no river of note and lives on wells and a stretched aquifer, so water is its limit. Leyda was unplantable until a pipeline brought Maipo river water across from the south at the end of the 1990s. The Pacific and the Humboldt Current set everything else.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Casablanca's grassy, grapefruit style and Leyda's sharper, saltier, more mineral one; the reference white of coastal Chile.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Citrus and white peach with firm acidity from Casablanca; tauter and more saline from Aconcagua Costa's schist and from Leyda.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Red cherry, raspberry and dried herb from Casablanca, darker and more savoury from Leyda and San Antonio.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Cool coastal Syrah from San Antonio and Casablanca: white pepper, olive and smoked meat at modest alcohol, a different grape from Colchagua's.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The grape of inland Aconcagua, structured and herbal, the base of the valley's historic blends.

grapes.name: Carménère
grapes.styles: A component of the Aconcagua blends and of Seña in particular, adding spice and red fruit to Cabernet.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Rounds out the inland reds; little of it near the coast.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A few coastal rows at Lo Abarca and Casablanca, dry, lime scented and sharply acidic.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: A Casablanca curiosity, lychee and rose at lower alcohol than Alsace.

wines.note: Grapefruit, cut grass, green capsicum and a mineral finish at high acidity, made in steel and drunk young; crab, oysters and goat's cheese salads.
Medium bodied, dark cherry and dried herb with a savoury, salty edge and fine tannin; serve cool with duck, salmon or roast pork.
Cabernet led with Carménère and other Bordeaux grapes, cassis and wild herb over fine, dusty tannin, raised in French oak; the icon style of Seña and Don Maximiano, built for lamb and beef.
White pepper, black olive and violet at 13 to 14 per cent, cooler and leaner than inland Syrah; think of a northern Rhône style for grilled meats and charcuterie.
Lemon, white peach and a little oak cream with the acidity to carry it; a reliable pour for roast chicken, cream sauces and richer fish.

made.viticulture: Casablanca's great enemy is frost: the basin collects cold air in spring, so growers use wind machines, sprinklers and site choice on the slopes, and the fight for water against the aquifer's limit shapes where anything can be planted. Vines are on vertical trellises at moderate density, drip irrigated, with leaf plucking timed to open the canopy once the fog lifts; Sauvignon Blanc is picked in several passes, early for the green and pungent notes, later for riper citrus. San Antonio and Leyda add wind, which thickens skins and lowers yield, and salt in the air near Lo Abarca. The season is long: Pinot Noir and Syrah here come in from late March into April, weeks after the same grapes inland. Inland Aconcagua is the opposite problem, heat and sun, answered by planting Cabernet on the cooler hillsides and slopes rather than the floor and by biodynamic farming on the Seña estate. Phylloxera is absent, so most vines stand on their own roots, with grafting used chiefly against nematodes in sandy soils.
made.winemaking: The coastal whites are made for precision: Sauvignon Blanc picked cold at night, pressed gently, fermented cool in steel and kept reductive on fine lees with no malolactic conversion, so the thiols and acidity hold. Chardonnay sees barrel or concrete, lees stirring and a measured share of new oak, with the schist wines of Aconcagua Costa kept lean. Pinot Noir gets a cold soak, partial whole bunch and older barrels, and the better houses pick it for savoury rather than sweet fruit. Coastal Syrah is often fermented with stems and raised in large oak to keep the pepper. Inland, the Cabernet blends follow the Bordeaux pattern: parcel by parcel ferments, long maceration, eighteen months or more in French barriques, a Carménère share for spice, and a final blend that must hold 75 per cent of any grape it names. The Berlin Tasting of 2004 was built on exactly that model.

law.classification: The Aconcagua viticultural region of Decreto 464 holds three subregions: Valle del Aconcagua, Valle de Casablanca and Valle de San Antonio. Panquehue is the Aconcagua valley's best-known area, and its coastal end is labelled Aconcagua Costa. Casablanca is a single subregion. San Antonio holds the zone of Leyda and, since the decree published on 25 May 2018, the area of Lo Abarca, which carries the Costa term and must be 85 per cent from the named ground. The position terms of 2011 earn their keep here: Aconcagua Costa names a climate wholly unlike the warm interior. Variety, vintage and origin need 75 per cent, 85 for Europe.

places.name: Aconcagua Valley
places.note: The valley of the Aconcagua river, named for the highest peak in the Americas across the border. Errázuriz planted at Panquehue in 1870; warm and dry inland, it is Cabernet country with Carménère and Syrah in support; its coast is a separate, cool world.

places.name: Panquehue
places.note: The historic heart of the interior, where Errázuriz was founded in 1870; hillside Cabernet and Carménère on clay and stone, the source of Don Maximiano.

places.name: Ocoa
places.note: A hillside site down the valley near Hijuelas, farmed biodynamically, that grows the Seña blend; an Advanced address.

places.name: Aconcagua Costa
places.note: The coastal stretch of the valley, a short way from the sea, with schist and slate bedrock rare in Chile; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah of real tension.

places.name: San Felipe and Los Andes
places.note: The upper valley towns towards the mountain pass to Argentina, warm and sunny, more table grapes than wine; useful only to place the valley on the map.

places.name: Casablanca Valley
places.note: The basin in the Coastal Range between Santiago and Valparaíso, first planted in 1982 by a Concha y Toro winemaker who saw what the fog could do. Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with cool Syrah; frost and water are its two limits.

places.name: Casablanca town
places.note: The valley's town, on the road from Santiago to the coast; the valley's wineries line the highway on either side of it.

places.name: Las Dichas
places.note: The western, coolest sector of the valley towards the sea, source of the sharpest Sauvignon Blanc and some of the best Pinot Noir.

places.name: The eastern end
places.note: The warmer eastern side of the basin nearer Santiago, where Syrah and Merlot ripen more easily and frost is less severe.

places.name: San Antonio Valley
places.note: The coastal subregion south of Casablanca around the port of San Antonio, the coldest of the three, planted only from the late 1990s. Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Syrah and Chardonnay with salt and pepper in the glass.

places.name: Leyda
places.note: The best known zone, on ridges about a dozen kilometres from the sea, planted once a pipeline brought Maipo river water; the name most lists use for San Antonio fruit.

places.name: Lo Abarca
places.note: A bowl four kilometres from the Pacific, home of Casa Marín, recognised as an area with the Costa term in 2018; saline Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling and peppery Syrah.

places.name: Rosario
places.note: The valley between Casablanca and San Antonio where Matetic farms biodynamically; its Syrah was among the first to show Chile's cool coastal style.

producers.name: Viña Errázuriz
producers.why: Founded at Panquehue in 1870, the valley's historic house, maker of Don Maximiano and the Las Pizarras coastal wines, and the organiser of the Berlin Tasting.

producers.name: Seña
producers.why: The Aconcagua icon blend begun in 1995 with Robert Mondavi, second in the 2004 Berlin Tasting; Cabernet with Carménère from a biodynamic hillside.

producers.name: Casa Marín
producers.why: Founded in 2000 at Lo Abarca, four kilometres from the sea, the estate that pushed Chilean Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah to the edge of the Pacific.

producers.name: Viña Leyda
producers.why: Founded in 1997, the house that built the pipeline from the Maipo river and planted the Leyda zone; its Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir named the place.

producers.name: Matetic
producers.why: The biodynamic estate at Rosario whose EQ Syrah showed that cool coastal Chile could make peppery, northern Rhône styled reds.

producers.name: Casas del Bosque
producers.why: A Casablanca estate, a reference for the valley's Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Veramonte
producers.why: One of the larger Casablanca houses, and a Sauvignon Blanc often met on export lists.

producers.name: Kingston Family Vineyards
producers.why: A Casablanca estate in the western hills known for Pinot Noir and cool Syrah, planted on the family's ranch.

exam: Separate the three valleys: warm inland Aconcagua for Cabernet blends, Casablanca for Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, San Antonio and Leyda for the sharpest coastal wines.
Casablanca's first planting in 1982 and its two hazards, frost and water.
Leyda is a zone of San Antonio, not of Casablanca, and the pipeline from the Maipo is why it exists.
Seña, Don Maximiano and the Berlin Tasting belong to Aconcagua; Viñedo Chadwick is the same family's Maipo wine.
Aconcagua Costa on schist, Lo Abarca's 2018 area and the Rosario valley are Advanced detail.
The Humboldt Current and fog as the reason a valley level with the Maipo is cool.
traps: Aconcagua and Casablanca share a lesson number in the atlas, not a climate; the inland valley is warm, the coastal basin is cool.
Leyda is a zone of the San Antonio valley; it is neither in Casablanca nor a synonym for it.
Seña was begun with Robert Mondavi of Napa, while Almaviva's partner is Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Bordeaux; both are Cabernet led, only Seña is Aconcagua.
Coastal Syrah here is peppery and lean; do not describe it as the dense, chocolatey Syrah of Colchagua.
Casablanca is west of Santiago in the Coastal Range, not on the coast itself; Lo Abarca and Leyda are the vineyards nearest the sea.
The Aconcagua river takes its name from the mountain, which stands across the border in Argentina, not in Chile.

cards.f: The three valleys of the Aconcagua region
cards.b: Aconcagua (the river valley, warm inland, schist coast), Casablanca (fog-cooled basin, whites and Pinot), San Antonio with its Leyda zone (coldest, nearest the sea).

cards.f: Casablanca: first planting and two hazards
cards.b: Planted in 1982 for the sea fog. Spring frost in the basin and scarce water from wells; it has no river.
A zone of San Antonio a dozen kilometres from the Pacific, dry until a pipeline brought Maipo river water at the end of the 1990s; Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Syrah.
Aconcagua's icon: Cabernet led with Carménère from a biodynamic hillside at Ocoa, begun in 1995 with Robert Mondavi, second in the 2004 Berlin Tasting.
Schist and slate near the coast, rare in Chile; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir of marked tension (the Las Pizarras wines).
San Antonio area created in 2018, four kilometres from the sea, Costa term, 85 per cent rule; Casa Marín's home.

cards.f: Coastal Chilean Syrah in three words
cards.b: Pepper, olive, restraint: whole bunch ferments, modest alcohol, large oak; San Antonio, Casablanca and Elqui, unlike inland Colchagua's style.

cards.f: Panquehue: which house, and since when
cards.b: Errázuriz founded there in 1870, the warm interior of the Aconcagua valley; the Don Maximiano blend is its flagship.

questions.q: In which year was the Casablanca valley first planted for wine?
questions.exp: Casablanca was planted in 1982 once the sea fog was understood as a cooling asset. 1870 is the founding of Errázuriz at Panquehue, 1994 the Carménère identification and 2004 the Berlin Tasting.

questions.q: Which valley holds the Leyda zone?
questions.exp: Leyda is a zone of the San Antonio valley, south of Casablanca and nearer the sea. It is irrigated with Maipo river water by pipeline, which is why Maipo is a tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: Which Napa producer was the original partner in the Aconcagua blend Seña?
questions.exp: Seña began in 1995 as a joint venture between Errázuriz and Robert Mondavi of Napa; the Chilean family later took sole control. Almaviva, the venture often confused with it, pairs the Mouton Rothschild company with Concha y Toro in the Maipo.

questions.q: Which white grape is Casablanca best known for?
questions.exp: Sauvignon Blanc is Casablanca's signature, grassy and citrus at high acidity, with Chardonnay close behind. Gewürztraminer is a Casablanca curiosity, Muscat of Alexandria belongs to the pisco north and old Itata vines, and Pinot Gris is a minor grape in Chile.

questions.q: What is the chief spring hazard for growers in the Casablanca basin?
questions.exp: The basin collects cold air at night in spring, so frost is the chronic threat and wind machines and sprinklers are standard; water scarcity is the valley's other limit but not a spring event.

questions.q: Which bedrock gives the Aconcagua Costa vineyards their character?
questions.exp: Aconcagua Costa sits on schist and slate, rare in a country of granite and alluvium; the Las Pizarras wines take their name from the slate. Limestone is Limarí's story, basalt belongs to volcanic soils further south.

questions.q: Which red grape is the Leyda zone best known for?
questions.exp: Leyda's cold, windy ridges a dozen kilometres from the Pacific make savoury, dark cherried Pinot Noir, with Syrah close behind. Carménère and Cabernet Sauvignon need the warmth of the Central Valley, and Malbec is a supporting red of Colchagua and Maule.

regions.name: Maipo Valley
regions.summary: The Maipo is Santiago's valley and the cradle of Chilean fine wine: the French cuttings of the 1850s were planted here, and the great houses, Cousiño Macul, Santa Rita, Concha y Toro, Carmen and Undurraga, still stand around the capital. Cabernet Sauvignon is the grape, and the address is the Alto Maipo, the Andean foothills at Puente Alto and Pirque, where stony river gravels and cold mountain night air give cassis, cedar and mint with fine tannin. Don Melchor, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick all come from Puente Alto. The valley warms and softens westward through Isla de Maipo and Talagante towards the Coastal Range. Study notes call it the Bordeaux of South America.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean: dry, sunny summers, winter rain of 300 to 400 millimetres, and little humidity. The Alto Maipo is cooled every night by air sliding down from the Andes, so the swing between day and night can pass twenty degrees and Cabernet keeps its acidity and its herbal lift. The middle valley around Isla de Maipo is warmer and more even; the western reaches towards Melipilla and María Pinto feel a touch of the sea. Spring frost and hail strike in some years, but the ripening season is long and reliable.
terroir.soils: Alluvial fans laid down by the Maipo and its tributaries. At Puente Alto and Pirque the soil is rounded stone and gravel over sand and a little clay, poor, free draining and low in organic matter, the Chilean answer to the Médoc's gravel. Further west the fans grade into deeper clay loam and sand, more fertile and warmer, where Carménère and Merlot ripen easily. Colluvial slopes of broken rock sit along the Andean foothills.
terroir.topography: The valley falls from the Andean foothills past the capital and runs west to the Coastal Range, losing height as it goes. The Alto Maipo is the eastern bench at 500 to 800 metres; Maipo Medio is the floor around Isla de Maipo, Talagante and Buin; Maipo Bajo or Pacific Maipo is the lower, western country towards Melipilla. Santiago itself sits in the middle and has swallowed much of the old vineyard, Macul included.
terroir.water: The Maipo river, fed by snowmelt, and its tributary the Mapocho through Santiago carry the irrigation, in canals dug in colonial times and now through drip lines. The wind that funnels along the valley is the reason the old estates planted lines of poplars as windbreaks, a sight that marks the valley.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The valley's identity: cassis, cedar, dried herb and a mint or eucalyptus note, with gravelly, fine tannin from the Alto Maipo and softer, riper fruit from the floor.

grapes.name: Carménère
grapes.styles: Ripens well on the warmer clay of Isla de Maipo and gives spice and red fruit to the Cabernet blends, including Almaviva.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Plummy, soft and used in the blends and the mid-priced reds of the middle valley.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: A small, growing part of the Puente Alto blends, adding floral lift and tobacco.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A seasoning grape in the Bordeaux-styled blends for colour and spice.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Full, dark and peppery from the foothills, a smaller planting than in Colchagua.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown mainly in the western, cooler reaches; the valley's whites are a footnote to its reds.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: A fresh, simple white from the Pacific side of the valley; not the Maipo's reason to exist.

wines.note: Full bodied yet fresh, cassis and blackcurrant leaf with cedar, mint and graphite over fine, dry tannin, raised in French oak and built to age twenty years; serve with lamb, prime rib or a bone-in steak.
Cabernet led with Carménère, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot in the Almaviva pattern: polished, dense and long, decant an hour and pour with roast beef or aged cheese.
Ripe red plum, paprika, dark chocolate and soft tannin from the warmer middle valley; a match for braised short rib, pork belly or dishes with smoked paprika.
The everyday face of the valley: cassis, a little oak, medium tannin and value, the by-the-glass red that carries the Maipo name round the world; burgers, grilled sausages, pepper steak.

made.viticulture: The Alto Maipo is planted on the stony bench between 500 and 800 metres, where the vines are trained on vertical trellises, drip irrigated through a dry summer and shielded from the valley's wind by the poplar lines that frame the old estates. Yields are kept low on the gravels, which give little of their own accord, and Cabernet hangs late into April to lose its pyrazine edge while the cold nights hold the acidity. Much of the Cabernet here descends from the nineteenth-century cuttings by mass selection and stands on its own roots, because phylloxera never came. On the middle valley floor the soils are richer and the crop larger, so the work is in limiting vigour and in picking Carménère two or three weeks after Merlot. The valley's other pressure is Santiago itself, which has grown over vineyards at Macul and Peñalolén and pushes the houses south and east. Eucalyptus and the mint note it is blamed for are a debate every taster meets here.
made.winemaking: Maipo Cabernet is made on the Bordeaux pattern as the nineteenth-century houses learned it and the 1990s refined it. Fruit is sorted, cold soaked, fermented in stainless steel or small oak with a measured extraction, then raised twelve to twenty months in French barriques, with the share of new wood falling in recent years as the houses chase freshness over polish. The icon wines, Don Melchor from 1987, Almaviva from 1996 and Viñedo Chadwick, are blended parcel by parcel, and Almaviva carries a Carménère share that Opus One, its Napa cousin, never does. The old vessel of the valley was the raulí vat, Chilean beech, which gave the old wines their traditional cast until stainless steel and French oak took over from the 1980s. Clay tinajas have returned for the heritage wines at De Martino. The law asks 75 per cent of any grape or vintage named, and the serious houses exceed it.

law.classification: Valle del Maipo is a subregion of the Valle Central region under Decreto 464, with no zones and nine areas: Santiago, Pirque, Puente Alto, Buin, Isla de Maipo, Talagante, Melipilla, Alhué and María Pinto. The trade's words Alto Maipo, Maipo Medio and Maipo Bajo are descriptions, not denominations, and the law's nearest equivalent is the 2011 position term: a Maipo Andes is the foothill wine, a Maipo Entre Cordilleras the floor. A label naming Puente Alto or Pirque must draw 75 per cent of its wine from that area. The Reserva words follow the national rules and say little; the house and the area say everything.
tiers: Valle Central
The region that holds the Maipo with Rapel, Curicó and Maule; a blend across them falls back to this name.
Valle del Maipo
The subregion, and the name on most bottles; the whole basin around Santiago from the Andes to the Coastal Range.
Áreas
Santiago, Pirque, Puente Alto, Buin, Isla de Maipo, Talagante, Melipilla, Alhué and María Pinto; an area name needs 75 per cent.
Maipo Andes
The position term for the foothill vineyards of Puente Alto, Pirque and Alto Jahuel; the trade's Alto Maipo.
Maipo Entre Cordilleras
The floor around Isla de Maipo, Talagante and Buin; the trade's Maipo Medio.
labels: Alto Maipo
A trade term for the Andean bench at 500 to 800 metres; the Cabernet address.
Puente Alto
The area that grows Don Melchor, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick.
Antiguas Reservas
Cousiño Macul's long-lived Cabernet, the old-school Maipo style.
Casillero del Diablo
Concha y Toro's global brand, named for the cellar legend at Pirque; a scale question, not a terroir one.

places.name: Alto Maipo
places.note: The Andean bench east and south east of Santiago, 500 to 800 metres up on stony alluvial fans, cooled nightly by mountain air. Chile's Cabernet address and the source of its three best-known icons.

places.name: Puente Alto
places.note: The area on the north bank of the Maipo where the river leaves the Andes: rounded stones over sand, cold nights, and the vineyards of Don Melchor, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick close to one another.

places.name: Pirque
places.note: Across the river from Puente Alto, the historic seat of Concha y Toro, founded in 1883, and the home of the Casillero del Diablo cellar; stony foothill Cabernet and the Haras de Pirque estate.

places.name: Macul
places.note: The eastern edge of Santiago where Cousiño Macul was founded in 1856; the city has absorbed most of the old vineyard, and the house has planted afresh at Buin.

places.name: Alto Jahuel
places.note: The foothill sector of Buin, south of the capital, with the Santa Rita and Carmen estates; classic cedar and cassis Cabernet of the old style.

places.name: Maipo Medio
places.note: The valley floor south and west of Santiago around Isla de Maipo, Talagante and Buin: deeper, warmer soils where Carménère, Merlot and rounder Cabernet grow, and the base of the big houses' volume wines.

places.name: Isla de Maipo
places.note: An island of land between arms of the river, warm clay and sand, home of De Martino since 1934 and of Tarapacá; the Carménère address of the Maipo.

places.name: Talagante
places.note: The area west of Isla de Maipo where Undurraga was founded in 1885; Cabernet, Carménère and Merlot on the floor.

places.name: Buin
places.note: The area south of Santiago whose foothill side is Alto Jahuel; the Cousiño Macul and Santa Rita vineyards stretch across it.

places.name: Maipo Bajo
places.note: The lower western valley towards the Coastal Range and the sea around Melipilla, María Pinto and Alhué, cooler by a degree or two from the Pacific; Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay join the reds here.

producers.name: Concha y Toro
producers.why: Founded in 1883 at Pirque, the giant of Chilean wine and the maker of Don Melchor, the first Chilean icon Cabernet, from Puente Alto since 1987.

producers.name: Almaviva
producers.why: The Puente Alto joint venture of Baron Philippe de Rothschild and Concha y Toro, first vintage 1996; Cabernet led with Carménère.

producers.name: Viñedo Chadwick
producers.why: A former polo field at Puente Alto whose 2000 vintage placed first in the Berlin Tasting of 2004; Cabernet Sauvignon from the Errázuriz family.

producers.name: Viña Santa Rita
producers.why: Founded in 1880 at Alto Jahuel; Casa Real is the traditionalist Maipo Cabernet and the 120 range its best-known brand.

producers.name: De Martino
producers.why: Founded in 1934 at Isla de Maipo, credited with the first wine labelled Carménère, in 1996, and a leader of Chile's return to old vines and clay vessels.

producers.name: Cousiño Macul
producers.why: Founded in 1856 at Macul on the edge of Santiago; Antiguas Reservas is the long-lived, old-school Maipo Cabernet by which the others are measured.

producers.name: Viña Carmen
producers.why: Founded in 1850, which claims the oldest brand in Chilean wine, at Alto Jahuel beside Santa Rita; Carmen bottled one of the first wines sold as Carménère after 1994.

producers.name: Undurraga
producers.why: Founded in 1885 at Talagante, one of the nineteenth-century houses, now known for its single-site T.H. range across the country's valleys.

producers.name: Pérez Cruz
producers.why: An Alto Maipo estate at Huelquén in the foothills of Paine, a reference for modern Andean Cabernet and Cabernet blends.

exam: Maipo means Cabernet Sauvignon, and Puente Alto in the Alto Maipo is the address: Don Melchor, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick.
Know the founding dates of the Santiago houses: Carmen 1850, Cousiño Macul 1856, Santa Rita 1880, Concha y Toro 1883, Undurraga 1885.
The two joint ventures: Almaviva is Rothschild and Concha y Toro in Puente Alto; Seña is Mondavi and Errázuriz in Aconcagua.
Alluvial gravels and cold Andean night air explain the Alto Maipo's structure and freshness; the mint note is the valley's tasting tell.
The nine areas and the Alto, Medio and Bajo split are Advanced detail; the position terms map onto them.
Isla de Maipo as the Carménère pocket, and De Martino's 1996 Carménère label, credited as the first, are worth a card.
traps: Puente Alto is cold Andean-edge ground, not a hot valley floor; the icon Cabernets are fresh, not jammy.
Alto Maipo is a trade term with no legal standing; Puente Alto and Pirque are the legal areas, and Maipo Andes is the lawful way to say foothill.
Almaviva's French partner is Baron Philippe de Rothschild, the Mouton house, not Lafite, which owns Los Vascos in Colchagua.
Viñedo Chadwick is a Maipo wine from the Errázuriz family; Seña, their other icon, is from Aconcagua.
Carmen, Carménère and Carmín de Peumo are three different things: a house of 1850, a grape, and a Concha y Toro wine from Cachapoal.
The Maipo is Chile's Bordeaux by reputation, but its gravels are river stones at the foot of the Andes, not the Médoc's Garonne deposits.

cards.b: Santiago's valley, the cradle of Chilean fine wine: Cabernet Sauvignon on Andean gravels at Puente Alto and Pirque, cooled by mountain night air; cassis, cedar, mint.
Don Melchor (Concha y Toro, from 1987), Almaviva (Rothschild and Concha y Toro, from 1996), Viñedo Chadwick (the Errázuriz family, first in the 2004 Berlin Tasting).

cards.f: Alto, Medio and Bajo Maipo: what each names
cards.b: Trade terms for the Andean bench (Puente Alto, Pirque, Alto Jahuel), the floor (Isla de Maipo, Talagante, Buin) and the western reaches (Melipilla, María Pinto, Alhué).

cards.f: The nine areas of the Maipo
cards.b: Santiago, Pirque, Puente Alto, Buin, Isla de Maipo, Talagante, Melipilla, Alhué, María Pinto.
Concha y Toro and Baron Philippe de Rothschild, the Mouton company, from the 1996 vintage; a Cabernet led blend with Carménère, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot from Puente Alto.

cards.f: Why Alto Maipo Cabernet stays fresh
cards.b: Stony, poor alluvial fans at 500 to 800 metres and cold air draining off the Andes each night: a twenty degree swing holds acidity and the herbal, minty lift.
Carmen 1850, Cousiño Macul 1856, Santa Carolina 1875, Santa Rita 1880, Concha y Toro 1883, Undurraga 1885.
Chilean beech, the traditional vat wood of the old houses, replaced by stainless steel and French oak from the 1980s onward.

questions.q: Which Maipo area grows Don Melchor, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick?
questions.exp: All three come from Puente Alto, the stony Alto Maipo bench where the river leaves the Andes. Isla de Maipo and Talagante are the warmer middle valley and Melipilla the western reaches.

questions.q: Which Bordeaux first growth's owners are Concha y Toro's partners in Almaviva?
questions.exp: Almaviva, first made in 1996, pairs Concha y Toro with Baron Philippe de Rothschild, the company behind Mouton Rothschild. Lafite's owners hold Los Vascos in Colchagua, the classic swap, and Margaux and Latour are simply other first growths.

questions.q: Which grape is the Maipo valley best known for?
questions.exp: Cabernet Sauvignon is the Maipo's identity, grown on the Alto Maipo gravels since the French cuttings of the 1850s; the valley is often called the Bordeaux of South America.

questions.q: Which soil underlies the best Cabernet vineyards of Puente Alto and Pirque?
questions.exp: Puente Alto and Pirque sit on rounded stones and gravel laid down by the Maipo where it leaves the Andes, poor and free draining. Limestone marks Limarí, decomposed granite the Coastal Range hills and schist the Aconcagua coast.

questions.q: Which Maipo area on the warmer valley floor is best known for Carménère?
questions.exp: De Martino was founded at Isla de Maipo in 1934, and the warm clay and sand of that middle-valley area ripen Carménère well; the house is credited with the first wine labelled Carménère, in 1996.

questions.q: Which house created Don Melchor, the Puente Alto Cabernet first made in 1987?
questions.exp: Concha y Toro, founded at Pirque in 1883, first made Don Melchor from Puente Alto in 1987, often called Chile's first icon Cabernet. Almaviva is its venture with the Mouton company, and Viñedo Chadwick belongs to the Errázuriz family.

questions.q: Which of the 2011 complementary terms may a label add for Puente Alto and Pirque?
questions.exp: Puente Alto and Pirque lie on the Andean bench, so their wine may be labelled Maipo Andes. Entre Cordilleras covers the floor around Isla de Maipo and Talagante, and Costa the side of a valley towards the sea; the terms describe position, not quality.

questions.q: What was Chile's traditional vat wood before stainless steel and French oak arrived?
questions.exp: Raulí, a Chilean beech, made the great vats of the nineteenth-century houses and shaped the old Maipo style until stainless steel and French barriques replaced it from the 1980s; chestnut, acacia and cherry are European cooperage woods.

regions.name: Rapel / Colchagua
regions.summary: Rapel is the legal valley south of the Maipo, and it is really two: Cachapoal to the north and Colchagua to the south, each a zone of the decree, and labels nearly always name the zone. This is Chile's big-red country. Colchagua grows ripe, generous Cabernet Sauvignon, Carménère, Syrah and Malbec, with Apalta, a horseshoe of hills near Santa Cruz, as its grand address: Clos Apalta, Montes Alpha M and Neyen come from there, and Purple Angel draws on it. Cachapoal's claim is Peumo, the warm clay pocket near Lake Rapel that many rank first for Carménère. Both valleys cool at their edges, towards the Andes at Los Lingues and towards the sea at Marchigüe and Paredones.

terroir.climate: Warm Mediterranean, hotter and sunnier than the Maipo in the centre of the basin, with more winter rain than Santiago and a long, dry ripening season that lets Carménère hang into May. The Andean side at Los Lingues and Alto Cachapoal is cooled by mountain air at night, and the western side at Marchigüe, Lolol and Paredones by the Pacific breeze that comes through the gaps in the Coastal Range after noon. Peumo, low and sheltered near the lake, is warm by day and mild by night.
terroir.soils: The floor of both zones is alluvial clay and gravel laid down by the Cachapoal and Tinguiririca rivers, fertile where the clay runs deep. The hillsides are granite and decomposed granite of the Coastal Range, poor and free draining, which is why Apalta's slopes make finer wine than the flat below. Red clay lies at Marchigüe towards the coast, and colluvial stone and volcanic material at the Andean edge. Peumo's deep clay holds water and warmth, the Carménère secret.
terroir.topography: The Rapel basin lies between the two cordilleras; the Cachapoal river drains its northern half past Rancagua and Peumo, the Tinguiririca its southern half past San Fernando and Santa Cruz, and they meet at Lake Rapel. Apalta is a horseshoe of hills opening south to the Tinguiririca off the Colchagua floor, sheltered on three sides, with slopes of several aspects that ripen more slowly than the flat. Westward the Coastal Range breaks into the rolling, red-soiled hills of Marchigüe and Lolol before the coast at Paredones.
terroir.water: The Cachapoal and Tinguiririca rivers, snow fed, feed the canals that irrigate the floor then join as the Rapel river, which gives the valley its legal name and is dammed at Lake Rapel. Drip lines are now the rule on the hills. Coastal fog touches only the western fringe.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The most planted grape: ripe cassis and black cherry, chocolate and sweet oak, softer and broader than the Maipo's; the base of Montes Alpha M.

grapes.name: Carménère
grapes.styles: The valley's signature: red plum, paprika, soy and dark chocolate with a touch of green when early, from Apalta's old vines and Peumo's warm clay; Clos Apalta, Purple Angel and Carmín de Peumo.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Dense, dark, chocolatey Syrah from the warm hills, the opposite of the coastal style; Montes Folly from the steepest Apalta slopes.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Old plantings in Colchagua, floral and plummy, bottled alone by Viu Manent and used in the blends.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Soft, round and widely planted on the floor; a blend partner and a value red.

grapes.name: Petit Verdot
grapes.styles: A seasoning for the Bordeaux blends and for Purple Angel, adding colour and spice.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Small plantings for the blends, with a few varietal wines from the Andean side.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Coastal Colchagua at Paredones makes crisp, saline Sauvignon Blanc under the Costa term.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: A new planting on the cool coastal hills; light, red fruited and savoury.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A little from the coast and the Andean foothills; the valley remains a red one.

wines.note: Full, dense and polished, red plum, dark chocolate, paprika and cedar with ripe tannin from old hillside vines and eighteen months of French oak; decant and pour with lamb shoulder or a peppered beef dish.
Ripe cassis and black cherry, mocha and sweet spice, broad and soft, the generous sibling of Maipo Cabernet; grilled ribeye, braised oxtail and barbecue sauces suit it.
The ripest expression of the grape: black plum, soy, tobacco and chocolate, velvety and long from Cachapoal's warm clay; pork belly, smoked meats, dishes with cumin and paprika.
Dark, chocolatey and full with blackberry and liquorice, more Barossa than Rhône in weight; venison, short rib and blue cheese.
A coastal surprise from Paredones: citrus, green herb and sea salt at high acidity, made in steel and drunk young with oysters and ceviche.

made.viticulture: Two Colchaguas grow side by side. On the floor the vineyards are large, trellised, drip irrigated and often machine harvested, and the work is in holding back vigour on deep clay to keep Cabernet and Merlot from tasting of the crop rather than the place. On the hills, planted in earnest only from the 1990s, the rows run up granite slopes in Apalta and Marchigüe, yields are small and the harvest is by hand; Apalta also holds old own-rooted Carménère and Cabernet, planted early in the twentieth century or before, that form the core of Clos Apalta and Neyen. Carménère is the valley's test of patience: it sets unevenly, carries pyrazine late and must hang two or three weeks past Merlot, often into May, to lose the green pepper and gain its paprika and plum. Biodynamic and organic farming has a long record here through Emiliana and Lapostolle, and the 2010 earthquake, centred off the Maule coast, damaged tanks and barrel stacks across the valley. Phylloxera is absent, so grafting is a choice made against nematodes, not a necessity.
made.winemaking: Colchagua built Chile's premium export style in the 1990s and 2000s: ripe fruit, long maceration, gravity-flow wineries on the Apalta hillside, and generous French oak, with the icons spending up to two years in barrique. Carménère is often co-fermented or blended with Cabernet for structure, since alone it can be soft; Purple Angel adds a Petit Verdot seasoning; Clos Apalta and Purple Angel are Carménère led while Montes Alpha M is Cabernet led. Micro-oxygenation and careful extraction tame the tannin, and the recent trend is towards earlier picking, less new wood and more precise, less jammy fruit. Peumo's Carménère is made as a single-vineyard wine for weight and velvet. Cono Sur at Chimbarongo was an early champion of the screwcap and of organic certification at scale, and the coastal whites are made cold and reductively. The law asks 75 per cent of any grape, vintage or area named, and the 2018 areas Apalta and Los Lingues hold to 85.

law.classification: Valle del Rapel is a subregion of the Valle Central under Decreto 464, divided into two zones, Valle del Cachapoal and Valle de Colchagua. Cachapoal's areas are Rancagua, Requínoa, Rengo and Peumo; Colchagua's are San Fernando, Chimbarongo, Nancagua, Santa Cruz, Palmilla, Peralillo, Lolol and Marchigüe. The decree published on 25 May 2018 added Apalta, the horseshoe near Santa Cruz, and Los Lingues, at the Andean foot, each requiring 85 per cent of its wine from the named ground. The 2011 position terms are common here: Colchagua Andes for the foothills at Los Lingues, Colchagua Costa for western communes towards the sea such as Paredones, Entre Cordilleras for the floor. Rapel itself appears mostly on blends drawn from both zones.
tiers: Valle del Rapel
The subregion of the Valle Central south of the Maipo; a label naming Rapel may blend Cachapoal and Colchagua fruit.
Valle del Cachapoal
The northern zone around Rancagua, with the areas of Rancagua, Requínoa, Rengo and Peumo; Carménère at Peumo, Cabernet at the Andean edge.
Valle de Colchagua
The southern zone around Santa Cruz and San Fernando, with eight areas from Chimbarongo to Marchigüe; the big-red valley of Chile.
Apalta
An area created in 2018 within Colchagua, the horseshoe of hills near Santa Cruz; 85 per cent rule.
Los Lingues
An area created in 2018 at the Andean foot of Colchagua near San Fernando; 85 per cent rule.
Peumo
An area of Cachapoal near Lake Rapel, warm and clay rich, the country's best Carménère ground.
labels: Colchagua Costa
Coastal Colchagua fruit from Paredones and the western hills; cooler whites and Pinot Noir.
Colchagua Andes
The foothill side at Los Lingues; Cabernet and Carménère with night cooling.
Clos Apalta
Lapostolle's Carménère led icon from old Apalta vines; clos is a brand word here, not a French appellation term.
Carmín de Peumo
Concha y Toro's single-vineyard Carménère from Peumo in Cachapoal; not to be confused with Viña Carmen.

places.name: Cachapoal Valley
places.note: The northern zone of Rapel around Rancagua, drained by the Cachapoal river. Its Andean foothills grow structured Cabernet, its lower reaches at Peumo the ripest Carménère in Chile; quieter in reputation than Colchagua but with the single most cited Carménère site.

places.name: Peumo
places.note: A warm, sheltered area on the lower Cachapoal near Lake Rapel with deep clay soils: the home of Carmín de Peumo and the ground that gives Carménère its long, even season.

places.name: Requínoa and Rengo
places.note: Areas on the valley floor and the Andean side south of Rancagua, where Alto Cachapoal Cabernet and Syrah grow on stony foothill soils with cold nights.

places.name: Millahue
places.note: A side valley on the Cachapoal's southern edge where the VIK estate planted a Bordeaux-styled blend from scratch in the 2000s; a Master-level address.

places.name: Colchagua Valley
places.note: The southern zone of Rapel along the Tinguiririca, centred on Santa Cruz and San Fernando: Chile's most famous red valley, with ripe Cabernet, Carménère, Syrah and Malbec from the floor and finer wine from the granite hills.

places.name: Apalta
places.note: A horseshoe of granite hills opening south off the valley floor near Santa Cruz, with old own-rooted vines; home of Clos Apalta, Montes and Neyen and an area in its own right since 2018.

places.name: Santa Cruz
places.note: The valley's wine town and an area of the decree, the centre of its wine route; the big houses sit around it and Apalta lies just to the north east.

places.name: Los Lingues
places.note: The Andean foothill area near San Fernando, created in 2018, where Casa Silva grows Carménère and Cabernet on stony colluvial soils.

places.name: Marchigüe
places.note: Rolling red-clay hills on the western side towards the coast, cooler and windier, planted from the late 1990s by Montes among others; fine Cabernet, Syrah and Carménère.

places.name: Paredones and Pumanque
places.note: The western communes of Colchagua towards the sea, where Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir grow under the Colchagua Costa term.

places.name: Chimbarongo
places.note: The southern area of Colchagua on the Curicó border, home of Cono Sur since 1993 and of large plantings of Cabernet and Merlot.

places.name: Peralillo and Lolol
places.note: Western areas between Santa Cruz and the coastal hills: Los Vascos at Peralillo, and the Lolol hills further west, cooled by the afternoon sea breeze.

producers.name: Viña Montes
producers.why: Founded in 1988, the house that planted Apalta's steep slopes maker of Alpha M, the Syrah Folly and the Carménère Purple Angel.

producers.name: Lapostolle
producers.why: Founded in 1994 by the Grand Marnier family; Clos Apalta, Carménère led from old hillside vines, is Chile's best-known Carménère icon.

producers.name: Concha y Toro
producers.why: Its Carmín de Peumo, from the warm clay of Peumo in Cachapoal, is a benchmark single-vineyard Carménère.

producers.name: Casa Silva
producers.why: An old Colchagua family house, known for Carménère from Los Lingues at the Andean foot and for pushing the valley to its coast at Paredones.

producers.name: Viu Manent
producers.why: A family house dating from 1935 with its estate in Colchagua; the house that kept old Malbec alive and bottles it on its own.

producers.name: Cono Sur
producers.why: Founded in 1993 at Chimbarongo within the Concha y Toro group, an early champion of organic certification and the screwcap at scale in Chile.

producers.name: Los Vascos
producers.why: The Peralillo estate the Lafite Rothschild company bought into in 1988, the first growth's counterpart to the Mouton joint venture in the Maipo.

producers.name: Emiliana
producers.why: The large organic and biodynamic house whose Coyam blend from Colchagua made certified farming a Chilean export story.

producers.name: Neyen
producers.why: An Apalta estate built on old own-rooted Carménère and Cabernet, among the oldest vines on the hill; one blend, and a reference for the hill's old vines.

exam: Rapel holds two zones, Cachapoal and Colchagua; know which is north and that labels name the zone.
Apalta is the Carménère address: Clos Apalta, Montes Alpha M and Neyen, with Purple Angel drawing on it; old vines on granite in a sheltered horseshoe.
Peumo in Cachapoal is the single most cited Carménère site and the home of Carmín de Peumo.
Why Carménère needs a long hang: pyrazine, two to three weeks after Merlot, picked into May.
The 2018 areas Apalta and Los Lingues and their 85 per cent rule are Advanced detail.
The four areas of Cachapoal and eight of Colchagua, and the Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes positions across the valley.
Los Vascos as Lafite's estate versus Almaviva as Mouton's venture: a classic distractor pair.
traps: Rapel is the legal valley and Colchagua a zone within it; a server who calls Colchagua a region of its own is not wrong at the table but is wrong on paper.
Apalta is an area within Colchagua, not a valley beside it, and its horseshoe of hills shelters the vines on three sides.
Clos Apalta is Carménère led; Montes Alpha M, Almaviva and Don Melchor are Cabernet led.
Colchagua Syrah is dense and chocolatey; the peppery, lean Chilean Syrah comes from the coast and the north.
Peumo is in Cachapoal, not Colchagua, and Carmín de Peumo is a Concha y Toro wine, not a Carmen wine.
Colchagua is warm and inland; its coast at Paredones is a recent exception, so do not file the valley with Casablanca.

cards.f: Rapel's two zones, north to south
cards.b: Cachapoal (Rancagua, Peumo) then Colchagua (San Fernando, Santa Cruz, Apalta). Labels name the zone; Rapel appears mostly on blends.
A horseshoe of granite hills near Santa Cruz, sheltered and slow ripening, with old own-rooted vines; Clos Apalta, Montes Alpha M, Folly and Neyen, Purple Angel in part. An area since 2018.
Cachapoal area near Lake Rapel, warm, sheltered, deep clay: Chile's best Carménère ground and the source of Carmín de Peumo.
It ripens two to three weeks after Merlot and carries green pyrazine until late; Colchagua picks it in late April or May for paprika, plum and chocolate.
Apalta, the horseshoe near Santa Cruz, and Los Lingues, at the Andean foot near San Fernando; each needs 85 per cent from the named ground. Published May 2018.

cards.f: The Colchagua icons: which grape leads each
cards.b: Clos Apalta and Purple Angel: Carménère led. Montes Alpha M: Cabernet led. Montes Folly: Syrah. Coyam: a biodynamic Colchagua blend.
San Fernando, Chimbarongo, Nancagua, Santa Cruz, Palmilla, Peralillo, Lolol, Marchigüe; plus Apalta and Los Lingues from 2018.

cards.f: Lafite in Chile: which estate, and where
cards.b: Los Vascos at Peralillo in Colchagua, which the Lafite company bought into in 1988. The Mouton company's venture is Almaviva in the Maipo.

questions.q: Which of the Rapel valley's two zones lies to the north?
questions.exp: Cachapoal, around Rancagua and Peumo, is Rapel's northern zone and Colchagua, around San Fernando and Santa Cruz, its southern. Teno and Lontué are the two zones of Curicó, the next valley south.

questions.q: Which Colchagua locality is a horseshoe of hills famous for Carménère?
questions.exp: Apalta, near Santa Cruz, is the granite horseshoe whose old vines grow Clos Apalta and Neyen; it became an area of the decree in 2018.

questions.q: Which Cachapoal area is the most cited site in Chile for Carménère?
questions.exp: Peumo, on the lower Cachapoal near Lake Rapel, is the warm clay pocket that ripens Carménère best and the source of Concha y Toro's Carmín de Peumo. Rancagua, Requínoa and Rengo are the zone's other areas, further up the valley.

questions.q: Which grape leads the blend of Clos Apalta?
questions.exp: Clos Apalta is Carménère led, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot in support, from old Apalta vines. Montes Alpha M from the same hill is Cabernet led and Montes Folly is Syrah.

questions.q: Which Bordeaux first growth's owners bought into Los Vascos in Colchagua in 1988?
questions.exp: The Lafite Rothschild company bought into Los Vascos at Peralillo in 1988. The other Rothschild in Chile is the Mouton company, partner in Almaviva in the Maipo, which the exam likes to swap.

questions.q: In which year were Apalta and Los Lingues gazetted as areas of Chile's origin decree?
questions.exp: A decree published on 25 May 2018 created Apalta and Los Lingues, with Lo Abarca and Licantén, each needing 85 per cent from the named ground. 1994 is Decreto 464 itself, 2004 the Berlin Tasting and 2011 the year of the position terms.

questions.q: How long after Merlot does Carménère usually ripen in Colchagua?
questions.exp: Carménère ripens two to three weeks after Merlot, which is why it tasted green when the two were picked together before 1994; Colchagua often harvests it in late April or May.

questions.q: Which house makes the Colchagua icon Clos Apalta?
questions.exp: Lapostolle, founded in 1994 by the family behind Grand Marnier, makes Clos Apalta from old Carménère led vines on the Apalta hill. Montes Alpha M and Neyen are its neighbours there, and Carmín de Peumo is Concha y Toro's.
