regions.name: Curicó / Maule
regions.summary: Curicó and Maule are the southern half of the Central Valley, and together they carry more vines than any other part of Chile. Curicó, with its zones of Teno and Lontué, is where the Torres family arrived in 1979 and the modern era began: Cabernet, Sauvignon Blanc and Carménère at scale. Maule, the largest single valley, is two countries: an irrigated floor of Cabernet, Merlot and Carménère along the Claro and Loncomilla rivers, and the dry-farmed secano of the Coastal Range around Cauquenes, where old bush-vine País and Carignan grow without a drop of irrigation. The Carignan planted after the 1939 earthquake is the valley's modern pride under the VIGNO banner, and its País is the country's past made new.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean still, but cooler and wetter than Colchagua, the winter rain rising from Curicó south through Maule, with a lower Coastal Range that lets more Pacific air in. Days are warm and nights cool, frost is a spring risk on the flat, and the dry summer lasts long enough to ripen Cabernet with ease. The secano's old vines ride out the drought on deep roots, and the slate hills at Empedrado near the coast are cool enough for Pinot Noir.
terroir.soils: Curicó's floor is alluvial clay, sand and gravel, deep and fertile, which is why it carries volume. Maule's Coastal Range is granite weathered to red and sandy soils, poor and dry, the ground of the secano's bush vines; the Andean foothills around San Clemente carry volcanic ash and clay; the river terraces are alluvial; and at Empedrado an outcrop of slate, unusual in Chile, has been terraced for Pinot Noir.
terroir.topography: Curicó is a broad, flat basin between the ranges. Maule opens wider still, from the Andes at Colbún and San Clemente past Talca and San Javier to the rolling granite hills of the Coastal Range at Cauquenes and the coast at Constitución, with the secano on the dry inland side of those hills. Elevation is modest everywhere, and the difference that matters is irrigated floor against dry hill.
terroir.water: The Teno and Lontué rivers join to form the Mataquito and water Curicó; the Maule, with the Claro, the Loncomilla and the Tutuvén, waters the Maule floor and is dammed at Lake Colbún. The secano has none of it: Cauquenes and its neighbours live on winter rain alone, which is the whole meaning of the word.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The most planted grape of both valleys: ripe, soft, cassis and plum at value prices from the floor, firmer from the foothills and the Loncomilla.

grapes.name: Carménère
grapes.styles: Widely planted on the warm floor for spicy, plummy reds and blends; later ripening than in Colchagua.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Old dry-farmed bush vines of the Maule secano, planted from the 1940s: dark, high acid, savoury reds of damson and dried herb, bottled under the VIGNO rules.

grapes.name: País
grapes.styles: Century-old bush vines in the secano make pale, light, rustic reds and pipeño, now made with care as a serious light red and as sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Curicó's volume white, fresh and simple; the old Sauvignonasse plantings have largely given way to true Sauvignon Blanc.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Soft, plummy and plentiful on the irrigated floor, a blend partner and a value varietal.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.styles: Old plantings in Maule and Curicó, floral and dark, sometimes bottled alone.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Grown beside País in the Cauquenes secano, pale and peppery; a Secano Interior grape.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A supporting white from the floor and the Colbún foothills.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Planted on the slate terraces at Empedrado near the coast for a cool, mineral red.

wines.note: Deep, dark and high in acidity, damson, black olive, dried herb and a rustic grip from dry-farmed bush vines of thirty years or more; serve with lamb, grilled sausages or a bean stew.
Pale, light and fresh, red berry, earth and a faint bitterness, low in tannin and alcohol, best lightly chilled with charcuterie, empanadas or roast chicken.
Crisp, simple citrus and herb at a friendly price, the by-the-glass white of many lists; salads, fried fish and shellfish.
Ripe cassis and plum with soft tannin and modest oak from the irrigated floor, firmer and more savoury from the Loncomilla hills; steak frites and barbecue.

The country wine of the south, young, cloudy and juicy from País or Cinsault, traditionally destemmed on the zaranda, fermented in open vats and sold within months; chilled, with street food and grilled meats.

made.viticulture: The irrigated floor of Curicó and Maule is Chile's engine room: vertical trellises, drip lines, mechanical harvest and yields set by the market, with the hazard of spring frost on the flat and of rot in a wet autumn. The secano is the opposite world. Around Cauquenes and across the dry inland side of the Coastal Range stand head-trained bush vines of País a century or more old and of Carignan planted after the 1939 Chillán earthquake, when the state encouraged the grape to give colour and acid to País. They are dry farmed on granite, ploughed by horse where the slopes allow, cropped low by nature and picked by hand and destemmed on the zaranda, the sieve across which the bunches are rubbed. VIGNO, the growers' association formed at the start of the 2010s, sets the rules for its Carignan: at least 65 per cent of the grape, dry-farmed bush vines of at least thirty years from the Maule secano, and two years of ageing before release. The Torres family's Chilean house, at Curicó since 1979, brought stainless steel and later terraced the slate at Empedrado for Pinot Noir. Phylloxera is absent, so the old vines stand on their own roots.
made.winemaking: Two cellars again. The volume houses of Curicó and the Maule floor ferment in stainless steel, use oak chips, staves or a short spell in barrel, and bottle Cabernet, Merlot, Carménère and Sauvignon Blanc for the by-the-glass trade, and Torres brought temperature-controlled stainless steel to Curicó in 1979. Sparkling wine has a long history here, with Valdivieso, founded in 1879 and now based at Lontué, its historic house. The secano's revival works the other way: País and Cinsault often fermented whole bunch or by carbonic maceration, in open raulí vats, concrete or clay tinajas, with no new oak, and bottled young and pale as pipeño or as a serious light red; a few houses make País sparkling by the traditional method. VIGNO Carignan is aged two years before release, usually in used barrels, large vats or other neutral vessels, so the grape's acidity and savoury depth show without oak sweetness. The law's 75 per cent rule applies to every grape, vintage and valley named, and Secano Interior may be written only for País and Cinsault from the listed dry-farmed communes.

law.classification: Valle de Curicó and Valle del Maule are subregions of the Valle Central under Decreto 464. Curicó holds two zones, Valle del Teno with the areas of Rauco and Romeral, and Valle del Lontué with the areas of Molina and Sagrada Familia, and since the decree published on 25 May 2018 the coastal area of Licantén, which carries the Costa term and needs 85 per cent. Maule holds three zones: Valle del Claro with Talca, Pencahue, San Clemente and San Rafael; Valle del Loncomilla with San Javier, Villa Alegre, Parral and Linares; and Valle del Tutuvén with Cauquenes. Secano Interior is a special denomination for País or Cinsault from listed dry-farmed communes of the southern Coastal Range. VIGNO is a private charter with no legal force. The 2011 position terms apply where the decree allows: Andes for the foothills, Costa towards the sea.
tiers: Valle de Curicó
The subregion south of Rapel: the zones of Teno and Lontué and the coastal area of Licantén; volume Cabernet, Sauvignon Blanc and Carménère.
Valle del Teno
Curicó's northern zone along the Teno river, with the areas of Rauco and Romeral.
Valle del Lontué
Curicó's southern zone along the Lontué, with the areas of Molina and Sagrada Familia; the historic cellars of San Pedro and Valdivieso.
Valle del Maule
The largest subregion by vineyard, south of Curicó, with the zones of Claro, Loncomilla and Tutuvén.
Valle del Claro
Maule's northern zone around Talca: the areas of Talca, Pencahue, San Clemente and San Rafael.
Valle del Loncomilla
Maule's central zone along the Loncomilla river: San Javier, Villa Alegre, Parral and Linares; granite hills on its western side.
Valle del Tutuvén
Maule's south-western zone with the single area of Cauquenes, the heart of the secano and of old País and Carignan.
Secano Interior
A denomination for País or Cinsault from the listed dry-farmed communes of the Coastal Range; no other grape may use it.
VIGNO
The Vignadores de Carignan charter: 65 per cent Carignan, dry-farmed bush vines of thirty years or more from the Maule secano, two years of ageing; a seal, not a law.
labels: Secano
Dry farmed, without irrigation; the word on a País or Carignan label that tells you where it grew.
Secano Interior
The protected term for País and Cinsault from the dry inland side of the Coastal Range.
VIGNO
The Carignan association's seal; expect old vines, dry farming and two years of age.
Pipeño
Young, unfiltered country wine of País or Cinsault, traditionally sold by the pipe or the demijohn.
Licantén
Curicó's coastal area created in 2018 with the Costa term.

places.name: Curicó Valley
places.note: The valley north of the Maule, flat and fertile, where the modern Chilean industry began in 1979; two zones along the Teno and Lontué rivers, large estates at Molina, and the coastal area of Licantén towards the sea.

places.name: Lontué
places.note: The southern zone with the areas of Molina and Sagrada Familia, home of San Pedro, founded in 1865, and of Valdivieso's sparkling cellars; San Pedro's Molina estate is a famously large single vineyard.

places.name: Teno
places.note: The northern zone along the Teno river with the areas of Rauco and Romeral; Cabernet, Merlot and Sauvignon Blanc on deep alluvial soils.

places.name: Licantén
places.note: The coastal area of Curicó near the mouth of the Mataquito, created in 2018 with the Costa term; a small, cool, new frontier.

places.name: Maule Valley
places.note: Chile's largest wine valley, from the Andes at Colbún to the coast at Constitución: Cabernet and Carménère on the irrigated floor, old dry-farmed País and Carignan in the granite hills of the secano, and slate at Empedrado.

places.name: Cauquenes
places.note: The area and town of the Tutuvén zone in the Coastal Range, the heart of the secano: century-old bush-vine País and the Carignan planted after 1939, dry farmed on granite, the VIGNO heartland.

places.name: Loncomilla
places.note: The central zone along the Loncomilla river with San Javier, Villa Alegre, Parral and Linares; granite hills on its western side grow structured Cabernet and some old Carignan.

places.name: Claro
places.note: The northern zone around Talca with Pencahue, San Clemente and San Rafael; the irrigated floor and the Andean foothills where Lake Colbún lies.

places.name: Empedrado
places.note: Slate hills near Constitución on the Maule coast, terraced by the Torres family for Pinot Noir; with Aconcagua Costa, one of Chile's rare slate vineyards.

places.name: Melozal and Caliboro
places.note: Hamlets of the Loncomilla secano near San Javier with old dry-farmed Carignan, País and Cabernet on granite; VIGNO ground.

places.name: Colbún and San Clemente
places.note: The Andean side of the Claro zone around Lake Colbún, cooler at night, where Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet grow on the foothill side of the valley.

producers.name: Torres Chile
producers.why: The Penedès family's Chilean house, at Curicó since 1979, which brought stainless steel to the country and later terraced Empedrado's slate for Pinot Noir.

producers.name: Viña San Pedro
producers.why: Founded in 1865 at Molina in the Lontué, one of the oldest and largest houses, maker of Cabo de Hornos, with its large estate at Molina.

producers.name: Valdivieso
producers.why: Founded in 1879, Chile's historic sparkling house at Lontué, now also known for its Caballo Loco solera-style red blend.

producers.name: Viña Bouchon
producers.why: A Maule family house of French origin at Mingre in the secano, a leader of the País revival with wines from vines that climb wild into the trees.

producers.name: Odfjell
producers.why: A VIGNO member with old dry-farmed Carignan at Cauquenes, founded by a Norwegian shipping family and farmed organically.

producers.name: Laberinto
producers.why: A small estate on the shore of Lake Colbún in the Maule Andes, the reference for cool foothill Sauvignon Blanc from the valley.

producers.name: Erasmo
producers.why: An estate founded by an Italian family at Caliboro in the Loncomilla secano, dry farming a red blend of Bordeaux grapes on granite.

exam: Curicó's two zones, Teno and Lontué, and Maule's three, Claro, Loncomilla and Tutuvén, with Cauquenes as the secano's heart.
The Torres arrival in 1979 at Curicó as the start of the modern era: stainless steel and the export mindset.
Carignan's 1939 story and the VIGNO rules: 65 per cent, thirty-year dry-farmed bush vines, Maule secano, two years of ageing.
Secano Interior as a legal term limited to País and Cinsault from the dry-farmed communes.
Maule as the largest valley by vineyard and the source of much of Chile's value Cabernet and Merlot.
Empedrado's slate and Licantén's 2018 area are Advanced detail; Melozal and Caliboro are Master-level addresses.
traps: Maule lies south of Curicó; the atlas names the pair north to south.
VIGNO is a growers' charter and seal, not a denomination of the decree; Secano Interior is the legal term and covers only País and Cinsault.
Carignan was planted in Maule after the 1939 earthquake to improve País, not as a fine wine project; it became one seventy years later.
País is the same grape as Mission and Listán Prieto, not a native Chilean vine.
Pipeño is a style and a tradition, not a grape or an appellation.
Curicó's old Sauvignon plantings were often Sauvignonasse, a lesser grape; the valley's true Sauvignon Blanc is a later replanting.

cards.b: Curicó: Teno (Rauco, Romeral) and Lontué (Molina, Sagrada Familia). Maule: Claro (Talca), Loncomilla (San Javier, Linares, Parral) and Tutuvén (Cauquenes).
At least 65 per cent Carignan, dry-farmed bush vines of thirty years or more from the Maule secano, two years of ageing before release. A private seal from the start of the 2010s.
Planted after the Chillán earthquake of 1939, with state encouragement, to give colour and acidity to País; the bush vines were left to age in the secano.
A protected term of the decree for País or Cinsault from the listed dry-farmed communes of the Coastal Range; forbidden for any other grape.

cards.f: What the Torres family began at Curicó in 1979
cards.b: The Torres family of Penedès brought temperature-controlled stainless steel to Chile and helped open the export era.
Young, cloudy País or Cinsault from the south, traditionally sold in bulk; now a serious chilled red on export lists.
Slate hills near Constitución on the Maule coast, terraced for Pinot Noir; one of Chile's rare slate vineyards.
The sieve the secano uses to destem by hand, rubbing the bunches across it; a word that marks a traditional País cellar.

questions.q: Which grape must make up at least 65 per cent of a wine under the VIGNO charter?
questions.exp: VIGNO is the Maule Carignan association: at least 65 per cent Carignan from dry-farmed bush vines of thirty years or more, aged two years. País and Cinsault are the Secano Interior grapes and Cabernet is the floor's volume red.

questions.q: After which year's earthquake was Carignan planted across the Maule secano?
questions.exp: The Chillán earthquake of 1939 led the state to encourage Carignan to improve País. Chile also suffered great earthquakes in 1960, 1985 and 2010, which makes each a plausible distractor.

questions.q: Which two grapes alone may carry the Secano Interior denomination?
questions.exp: Decreto 464 reserves Secano Interior for País or Cinsault from the dry-farmed communes of the Coastal Range; a Carignan or Cabernet from the same hills cannot use the term.

questions.q: In which year did the Torres family begin making wine at Curicó?
questions.exp: Torres arrived at Curicó in 1979 with stainless steel and an export mindset. 1865 is San Pedro's founding at Molina, 1988 is Montes and 1994 is Lapostolle and the Carménère identification.

questions.q: Which Maule zone holds the single area of Cauquenes?
questions.exp: Cauquenes is the only area of the Tutuvén zone, in the Coastal Range secano. Claro is around Talca, Loncomilla around San Javier and Linares, and Lontué is a zone of Curicó.

questions.q: What does the word secano mean on a Chilean label?
questions.exp: Secano means dry farmed: the vines live on winter rain alone with no irrigation, as in the Cauquenes hills of Maule. Secano Interior is the legal denomination built on the word, reserved for País and Cinsault.

questions.q: Which rock underlies the terraced Pinot Noir vineyard at Empedrado?
questions.exp: Empedrado near Constitución is an outcrop of slate, rare in Chile, terraced for Pinot Noir. Granite is the usual rock of the Coastal Range secano, limestone belongs to Limarí and basalt to the volcanic foothills.

questions.q: Which two zones make up the Curicó valley?
questions.exp: Curicó divides into Teno in the north, with Rauco and Romeral, and Lontué in the south, with Molina and Sagrada Familia. Cachapoal and Colchagua make up Rapel, Claro and Loncomilla are two of Maule's three zones, and Leyda and Lo Abarca lie in San Antonio.

regions.name: Itata / Bío Bío
regions.summary: Itata and Bío Bío are the two valleys of Chile's southern region, the Sur, with Malleco a third further south again. Itata, around Chillán and the hills towards the coast, is among the oldest wine country in Chile, planted within a generation of the Spanish settlement of Concepción in 1550, and its hills still carry head-trained País, Cinsault and Moscatel of great age, dry farmed on granitic sand. Bío Bío, along the great river to the south, is cooler, wetter and windier, and grows Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc beside its own old País. The south joins Chile's past and its newest fashion: pipeño, clay tinajas and bush vines beside cool aromatic whites.

terroir.climate: Cool and wet by Chilean measure. Itata receives around 1,000 millimetres of rain a year and Bío Bío more, falling mostly in winter but with a real risk of rain at harvest; summers are warm by day and cold at night, the growing season is long, and the wind off the Pacific and down the Bío Bío valley is constant. Frost is a spring hazard in Bío Bío, and fungal pressure is higher than anywhere north. Dry farming works because the winter fills the soil.
terroir.soils: Itata's hills are decomposed granite weathered to coarse sand rich in quartz, with red clay beneath; poor, free draining and the reason old vines could survive without irrigation. Bío Bío's floor is alluvial sand and gravel left by the river, with volcanic ash soils, the trumao, on the terraces and foothills. Malleco's plateau around Traiguén is red volcanic clay over gravel.
terroir.topography: Itata is rolling coastal hill country between Chillán and the sea, 100 to 400 metres high, with vineyards on slopes around Guarilihue, Ránquil, Portezuelo, Coelemu and Quillón. Bío Bío is a broad valley along the river of that name at 37 to 38 degrees south, with vineyards near Mulchén, Negrete and Yumbel on the flat and the terraces. Malleco, at Traiguén, is an open, rolling plateau in the Araucanía, Chile's southernmost serious vineyard until recent plantings further south.
terroir.water: The Itata and Bío Bío rivers drain the region, the Bío Bío among the longest in Chile, and the winter rain that feeds them is why the south needs little irrigation. The Pacific is near at Itata's western edge and sends fog and wind inland; the Andean lakes and volcanoes to the east feed the Bío Bío's cold flow.

grapes.name: País
grapes.styles: The old grape of Itata and Yumbel, head-trained bush vines of a century or more: pale, light, earthy reds, pipeño and, with care, serious chilled wine.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.styles: Planted in Itata in the 1940s after the earthquake; juicy, peppery, pale reds from old bush vines, the south's modern calling card.

grapes.name: Muscat
grapes.styles: Moscatel de Alejandría from old Itata vines: dry, floral, grapey whites, often fermented on the skins for an orange style.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Bío Bío's speciality white, dry and lime scented with sharp acidity; Mulchén is its best-known source.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: A Bío Bío aromatic at lower alcohol and higher acidity than Alsace; lychee and rose.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Taut, mineral Chardonnay from Bío Bío and from the Malleco plateau, where Sol de Sol set the standard.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Light, red fruited, savoury reds from Bío Bío and Malleco, slow ripening in the cool and wet.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Crisp and green from Bío Bío's cool floor; a smaller planting than in the coastal north.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: A few old dry-farmed plots in Itata beside the País, dark and high in acid.

wines.note: Pale ruby, strawberry, white pepper and dried herb, light tannin and bright acidity from old bush vines, often whole bunch and unoaked; serve cool with charcuterie, grilled fish or pork.
Light, pale and earthy, red currant and a faint bitter note at modest alcohol, made in old vats or clay; chilled with empanadas, roast chicken and tomato dishes.
Dry Moscatel de Alejandría fermented on its skins: orange peel, jasmine, grape and a tannic grip from old vines; pour with spiced dishes, cured fish and aged cheese.
Dry, lime, green apple and wet stone with sharp acidity and a little petrol with age; raw bar, Thai dishes and pork with apples.
Lean and mineral from the cold plateau at Traiguén, citrus and struck match over firm acidity, barrel fermented with restraint; scallops, roast chicken, cream sauces.
The south's country wine, young, cloudy and juicy from País or Cinsault, sold within months of harvest; chilled, with street food, sausages and grilled meats.

made.viticulture: Itata is farmed much as it was two centuries ago. Head-trained bush vines of País, Cinsault and Moscatel, many over a hundred years old, stand ungrafted on the sandy granite slopes, dry farmed, ploughed by horse because the hills are steep and the plots small, and cropped lightly because the soil gives little. Harvest is by hand, and the bunches are destemmed on the zaranda, the sieve across which they are rubbed. The valley's social story matters: smallholders long sold their grapes to the bulk trade at prices that barely paid, and pine and eucalyptus plantations have replaced many old vineyards, so the revival since about 2010 has been a rescue as much as a fashion. Bío Bío is a different farm: trellised rows of Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir planted from the 1990s on the flat and the terraces, where rain at harvest, spring frost and rot are the hazards, the wind keeps canopies dry, and ripening runs into late April. Malleco's plateau is colder again, with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir planted on red volcanic clay at the edge of the possible.
made.winemaking: Pipeño is the south's native method: grapes destemmed on the zaranda, fermented with wild yeast in open raulí vats or clay tinajas, pressed by hand and drunk young and cloudy, traditionally sold by the pipe and the demijohn. The modern houses keep the frame and refine it: whole-bunch or carbonic ferments for Cinsault and País, no new oak, concrete, old barrels or tinajas, low alcohol and early bottling, so the wines are pale, fresh and chilled on a list. Moscatel is pressed straight for a dry aromatic white or left on its skins for an orange wine of real grip. Bío Bío's whites are made cold and reductive in steel, Riesling dry or off dry, Gewürztraminer dry, and the better Chardonnay sees barrel fermentation with lees and a careful share of new oak, the Sol de Sol model from Malleco. Pinot Noir is given a cold soak, gentle extraction and older wood. The 75 per cent rule applies and Secano Interior may be written only for País and Cinsault.

law.classification: The Sur viticultural region of Decreto 464 holds three subregions: Valle del Itata with the areas of Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo and Coelemu; Valle del Bío Bío with the areas of Yumbel and Mulchén; and Valle del Malleco with the area of Traiguén. South of it the Austral region, with the Cautín and Osorno valleys and, since an amendment published in May 2025, Chiloé, covers the young plantings of the far south. Secano Interior, the denomination for dry-farmed País and Cinsault, reaches into this region's Coastal Range communes, and a bottle from Guarilihue or Yumbel usually names the valley alone. Variety, vintage and origin need 75 per cent; the old smallholder wines usually hold to one grape anyway.
tiers: Región vitícola del Sur
The southern region of the decree, holding Itata, Bío Bío and Malleco; the cool, wet, dry-farmed end of the Chilean map.
Valle del Itata
The subregion around Chillán and the coastal hills with the areas of Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo and Coelemu; old País, Cinsault and Moscatel.
Valle del Bío Bío
The subregion along the river with the areas of Yumbel and Mulchén; aromatic whites, Pinot Noir and old País.
Valle del Malleco
The southernmost subregion of the Sur with the area of Traiguén; Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on a cold plateau.
Región vitícola Austral
The region south of Malleco with the Cautín and Osorno valleys and, since May 2025, Chiloé; a Master-level footnote for the young cool vineyards of Chile's far south.
Secano Interior
The denomination for País or Cinsault from the listed dry-farmed communes, which include Itata's dryland hills.
labels: Pipeño
Young, cloudy País or Cinsault from the south, the farmhouse wine now on export lists.
Tinaja
A clay vessel of the old south, used for fermentation and storage; it adds no wood character.
Guarilihue
A hamlet of old vines in the Itata hills near Coelemu, often named on labels though it is no area of the decree.
Sol de Sol
Viña Aquitania's Malleco Chardonnay from Traiguén, the wine that put the far south on the map.

places.name: Itata Valley
places.note: The oldest wine country in Chile, around Chillán and the coastal hills towards Concepción, where the Spanish planted vines in the sixteenth century. Granitic sand, dry farming, head-trained bush vines of País, Cinsault and Moscatel, and a revival led by a few houses since about 2010.

places.name: Guarilihue
places.note: A hamlet in the hills near Coelemu with some of the valley's oldest Cinsault, País and Moscatel vines on steep granitic sand; the Itata name most often seen on a serious label.

places.name: Portezuelo
places.note: An area of the decree in the heart of the dryland hills, old bush vines and smallholder cellars; the Secano Interior country.

places.name: Coelemu
places.note: An area of the decree on the lower Itata near the coast, cooler and foggier, with old Moscatel and Cinsault on the slopes.

places.name: Quillón
places.note: An area of the decree on the eastern side towards the Central Valley, warmer, with País and Cinsault on sandy hills.

places.name: Chillán
places.note: The regional city and an area of the decree, the eastern gateway to the valley; the 1939 earthquake that reshaped the south's vineyards is named for it.

places.name: Ránquil and Ñipas
places.note: The commune of Ránquil and its town of Ñipas, in the dryland hills between Quillón and Coelemu, with century-old País and Cinsault, home to several of the revival's small producers.

places.name: Bío Bío Valley
places.note: The valley of the great river south of Itata, cool, wet and windy, planted from the 1990s to Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc on the flat and the terraces, with old País at Yumbel on its northern edge.

places.name: Mulchén
places.note: An area of the decree on the upper valley near the Andes, where Riesling and Gewürztraminer plantings, Cono Sur's among them, made Bío Bío's name for aromatic whites.

places.name: Yumbel
places.note: An area of the decree at the valley's northern edge with old dry-farmed País and a pipeño tradition, dry-farmed País country.

places.name: Negrete
places.note: A commune on the valley floor near Mulchén with cool-climate plantings on river terraces.

places.name: Malleco Valley
places.note: The southernmost subregion of the Sur, a cold, open plateau around Traiguén in the Araucanía, where Viña Aquitania's Sol de Sol Chardonnay proved the far south could make serious wine; Pinot Noir follows.

places.name: Austral region
places.note: The Cautín and Osorno valleys south of Malleco, with Chiloé added in 2025, where houses such as Casa Silva at Lago Ranco have planted Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling at the cold edge of Chilean viticulture.

producers.name: De Martino
producers.why: The Maipo house whose old-vine Cinsault and País from Itata, fermented in clay tinajas, led the south's revival on export lists.

producers.name: Clos des Fous
producers.why: A partnership of soil scientists and winemakers working extreme sites, including Itata's granite and the far south, in search of cool, pale, mineral wines.

producers.name: Rogue Vine
producers.why: An Itata project built on smallholder vineyards, bottling old-vine Cinsault, País and Moscatel at low alcohol.

producers.name: A Los Viñateros Bravos
producers.why: An Itata house dedicated to the brave grape growers of the dryland hills, with Cinsault, País and Moscatel from single granite slopes.

producers.name: Cono Sur
producers.why: The Concha y Toro group's cool-climate house, whose Mulchén vineyards in Bío Bío grow some of Chile's best-known Riesling and Gewürztraminer.

producers.name: Viña Aquitania
producers.why: A Maipo house founded with Bordeaux partners whose Sol de Sol Chardonnay from Traiguén in Malleco opened the far south.

producers.name: Cacique Maravilla
producers.why: A family cellar at Yumbel in Bío Bío with vines said to go back to the eighteenth century, known for traditional pipeño.

exam: Itata lies north of Bío Bío; Malleco is further south, and the Austral region beyond it.
Itata means old vines: dry-farmed bush-vine País, Cinsault and Moscatel on granitic sand, among the oldest vineyard land in Chile.
Bío Bío means cool aromatic whites, Riesling and Gewürztraminer at Mulchén, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.
The areas of the Sur are Advanced detail: Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo and Coelemu; Yumbel and Mulchén; Traiguén.
Pipeño, the tinaja and the zaranda as the south's traditional cellar, and why the modern wines are pale, chilled and unoaked.
Sol de Sol from Malleco as the wine that proved the far south.
traps: Itata is among Chile's oldest vineyard land, not its newest, even though its wines reached export lists only in the 2010s.
Cinsault in Itata dates from the 1940s, after the earthquake; País is the sixteenth-century grape.
Bío Bío is not Burgundy of the south: its reputation rests on Riesling and Gewürztraminer first, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay following.
Guarilihue is a hamlet on labels, not an area of the decree; Coelemu and Portezuelo are the legal names around it.
Pipeño is a style of young, unfiltered wine, not an appellation and not a grape.
Malleco and the Austral region are different tiers: Malleco is a subregion of the Sur, Cautín and Osorno belong to the Austral region.

cards.b: Among Chile's oldest vineyard land, around Chillán and the coastal hills: dry-farmed bush-vine País, Cinsault and Moscatel of a century or more on granitic sand, revived since about 2010.
The cool, wet, windy valley south of Itata: Riesling and Gewürztraminer at Mulchén, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, with old País at Yumbel.

cards.f: The three subregions of the Sur, north to south
cards.b: Itata, Bío Bío, Malleco. The Austral region (Cautín, Osorno and, since 2025, Chiloé) lies south again.

cards.f: The areas of Itata, Bío Bío and Malleco
cards.b: Itata: Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo, Coelemu. Bío Bío: Yumbel, Mulchén. Malleco: Traiguén.
The south's farmhouse wine: País or Cinsault destemmed on the zaranda, wild ferment in raulí or clay, pressed by hand, drunk young and cloudy, once sold by the pipe.
Around 1,000 millimetres of winter rain fills deep granitic sand, and century-old bush vines reach it with deep roots; no river is needed.

cards.f: Sol de Sol: what it is and where it grows
cards.b: Viña Aquitania's Chardonnay from Traiguén in Malleco, the wine that proved the far south of Chile; lean, mineral, barrel fermented.

cards.f: When and why Cinsault came to Itata
cards.b: Planted in the 1940s after the 1939 Chillán earthquake, as Carignan was in Maule; now the valley's juiciest old-vine red.

questions.q: Which white grape do Itata's old bush vines yield for dry and skin-fermented whites?
questions.exp: Moscatel de Alejandría, Muscat of Alexandria, grows on Itata's old dry-farmed bush vines and makes dry, floral whites, often left on the skins for an orange style. The same grape is a pisco variety in the north.

questions.q: Which aromatic white grape is Bío Bío's best-known speciality?
questions.exp: Riesling, with Gewürztraminer beside it, is Bío Bío's speciality, dry and lime scented from the cool, wet valley, notably at Mulchén. Viognier is a minor Chilean planting, Albariño is Galicia's grape and Torrontés is Argentina's aromatic white.

questions.q: What is the name of the south's young, cloudy country wine made from País or Cinsault?
questions.exp: Pipeño is the farmhouse wine of Itata, Bío Bío and Maule: destemmed on the zaranda, wild ferment, pressed by hand and drunk within months, traditionally sold in bulk by the pipe.

questions.q: Which viticultural region of Decreto 464 holds Itata, Bío Bío and Malleco?
questions.exp: The Sur region holds the three southern subregions. The Austral region lies further south with Cautín, Osorno and Chiloé, the Valle Central ends at Maule and Aconcagua is the coastal north of Santiago.

questions.q: Which vessel of clay do the traditional cellars of the south use for fermentation and storage?
questions.exp: The tinaja is the clay jar of the old Chilean south, used for pipeño and revived by De Martino and others; it breathes a little and adds no wood character.

questions.q: In which decade was Cinsault planted across the Itata hills?
questions.exp: Cinsault came to Itata in the 1940s after the Chillán earthquake of 1939, the same push that planted Carignan in Maule. The 1850s brought French grapes to the Maipo, the 1980s planted Casablanca and the 2010s were the revival.

questions.q: Which subregion lies furthest south in the Sur region?
questions.exp: Malleco, around Traiguén, is the Sur's southernmost subregion and the home of the Sol de Sol Chardonnay. Itata and Bío Bío lie north of it, and Cautín belongs to the Austral region beyond.
